cls: Dietary fat / nutritional supplement (emollient, source of monounsaturated fat)
pharm: Rich in monounsaturated fatty acids (chiefly oleic acid) and minor antioxidant polyphenols; acts as a dietary energy source, emollient, and demulcent rather than via a defined receptor.

summary: Olive oil is a dietary fat obtained from the fruit of Olea europaea, composed mainly of monounsaturated oleic acid with smaller amounts of polyunsaturated and saturated fats and minor polyphenol antioxidants. It is used as a food, a component of heart-healthy (Mediterranean-style) diets, a skin emollient, and to soften earwax. It is a nutritional supplement rather than an FDA-approved drug. It is generally very safe; the main considerations are its high caloric density and rare allergy. The FDA has permitted a qualified health claim that limited evidence suggests oleic acid from olive oil may reduce coronary heart disease risk when it replaces saturated fat.
indications: Dietary source of monounsaturated fat as part of a heart-healthy diet (supplement/food)
Topical emollient for dry skin (traditional/cosmetic use)
Softening and aiding removal of cerumen (earwax) - traditional use

Substitute for saturated fats (butter, lard) to support cardiovascular benefit

Account for its calorie density (~120 kcal per tablespoon) in weight/diet planning
moa: Olive oil acts chiefly as a dietary fat and emollient rather than through a specific pharmacologic receptor. Its high monounsaturated fatty acid (oleic acid) content, when substituted for saturated and trans fats, is associated with favorable effects on serum lipids (lowering LDL cholesterol). Minor constituents such as polyphenols (e.g., hydroxytyrosol, oleocanthal) and vitamin E have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Topically, the oil forms an occlusive layer that reduces transepidermal water loss; in the ear it softens cerumen by lubrication.

preg: Olive oil is a common dietary food and is considered safe in normal dietary amounts during pregnancy. No special precautions are needed beyond usual balanced nutrition.
lact: Olive oil is a normal dietary food and is considered safe during breastfeeding in usual dietary amounts.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed; olive oil is a dietary food without significant renal handling concerns.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed; olive oil is a dietary fat metabolized through normal lipid pathways.

minor: Very large dietary fat intake could modestly affect absorption timing of some fat-soluble medications, but no clinically important interactions are established
May have mild additive effects on blood lipids with lipid-lowering diets
interactions.food: Itself a food; best used in place of saturated fats within a balanced diet.

rare: Lipoid pneumonia if aspirated (e.g., misuse as nasal/oral lubricant in at-risk patients)

pearls: Dietary supplement/food, not an FDA-approved drug; data here reflect nutritional and traditional use plus an FDA qualified health claim

missed: Not applicable as a strict medication schedule. If using olive oil for a specific purpose (e.g., earwax softening), simply resume the directed routine; there is no need to make up a missed application.
overdose: Excessive oral intake mainly causes gastrointestinal upset and loose stools and contributes excess calories. There is no specific toxicity or antidote; manage supportively and moderate intake.
